1:
Clarke and Ellicott both object that the name of God is not in the Greek of the opening wish. The clause that follows is genuinely ambiguous, and the voices take opposite sides with full knowledge of each other. Chrysostom reads it as an affirmation, that they do indeed bear with him, and finds the shift eloquent: to say would that is to put the matter at their disposal, while to assert it outright is to confide greatly in their affection. Ellicott agrees, and traces a movement of feeling, indignation prompting the wish and the memory of their loyalty then softening it. Calvin knows Chrysostom's reading, grants that the Greek word is ambiguous and either sense suits well enough, and nevertheless follows the older Latin interpreter in taking it as a command. Robertson observes only that the two forms are identical. Ellicott then makes something larger of the wording: two catch-words run through the section, bearing with and folly, one occurring five times and the other eight, from which he infers that Titus had reported the opponents at Corinth saying something like, we can bear with him no longer, his folly is becoming intolerable.

Chrysostom answers the charge of vainglory before it is made: a man who remembers sins that God has forgotten, and calls himself unworthy of the very name of apostle, is plainly not speaking for the sake of glory. Henry puts it from the other side, that it is as much against the grain for a humble man to speak in his own praise as for a proud man to acknowledge his infirmities; Gill adds that the necessity was forced on him.

On the jealousy itself Barnes takes the phrase as a Hebraic superlative, the divine name marking whatever is signally great, as when the mountains of God are meant for very lofty mountains, so that the sense is a vehement attachment; Calvin distinguishes two kinds of jealousy, the one springing from self-love and of a perverse nature, the other cherished on God's account, and observes that many are zealous for themselves and not for God; Ellicott paraphrases it as a jealous care after the pattern of God's own. What part the apostle claims in the marriage they do not agree. Clarke takes him for the groomsman, comparing the Hebrew paranymphs and the Spartan magistrates who had charge of maidens; Gill calls him the friend of the bridegroom, and Calvin says One alone is the bridegroom of the church and all ministers are his friends, as the Baptist said of himself. Ellicott denies this: the verb properly describes the act of the father who gives his daughter in marriage, so that the claim is to be the father of the Corinthian church.

The fear that follows turns on the serpent. Clarke derives the word for subtlety from doing all work, a versatility that accommodates itself to the prejudices of those it deals with, and Ellicott renders it the activity of a man ready for anything, noting that it is not the word the Greek Old Testament uses there. Robertson remarks that this is the only mention of the serpent in Eden anywhere in these letters. Barnes warns that the tempter adapts his temptations to the character of the tempted. Wesley draws a sharper inference, that since Eve was simple and ignorant of evil we might be tempted even if there were no sin in us. Calvin makes the gospel the written contract by which the spiritual marriage is confirmed, as marriages among men are secured by written contracts, and Ellicott reports that many of the better manuscripts add chastity to simplicity, and some reverse the order.
4:
Ellicott presses the change of adjective, that the spirit and the gospel are called a different one where the Jesus is called another, and conjectures that the opponents preached a Christ who headed a Jewish kingdom and required circumcision as the condition of entering it, while the different spirit points to a counterfeit inspiration. Robertson accepts the distinction but will not insist on it, holding that any other Jesus is a rival and therefore wrong. The clause that closes the verse divides them. Barnes sets out three constructions, the serious one that if a better Saviour could be preached there would be propriety in receiving him, the ironical one that they cannot bear with the apostle but bear easily with anyone else, and a third that would read the last word as me rather than him; he decides for the first, and Clarke reports the same two and decides the same way. Wesley takes it seriously too and adds that the case is impossible. Calvin turns it into a reproach: had they brought another Christ or gospel or Spirit he would approve their regard for them, but since they conferred nothing he had not given already, what gratitude is it to adore men to whom nothing is owed while despising the man through whom God bestowed so much? Robertson alone hears irony, that they hold themselves back from the newcomer well enough.

Who the very chiefest apostles are is the sharpest question in the passage. Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke and Calvin all take them for the true apostles: Henry says the office was equal in all of them though the men differed as stars differ in glory, Calvin that God honoured this apostleship with marks of favour no less distinguished than John's or Peter's, and Barnes that the evidence of a commission from God was as good. Ellicott denies this with some heat, holding that the tone of the passage should have made such a reading impossible and calling it the insanity of controversy to suppose the words bear on the primacy of Peter; he renders the compound as apostles-extraordinary, an ironical coinage for the false teachers, and Robertson follows him with super apostles. Calvin adds the moral he draws from the comparison, that wherever we recognise the gifts of God we must there reverence God himself.

The confession of rude speech is handled with care by everyone. Barnes takes the word as meaning a plain unlettered person and thinks the apostle partly admits the charge, then meets the obvious objection: the endowment of the Spirit enabled the apostles to speak languages they had never learned and did not perfect them in one learned in childhood, so that the provincial Greek of his native place remained his. Clarke says the same more broadly, that the Spirit in general left them to their own language and prevented only equivocal expression. Calvin divides doctrine as a man is divided, into the thing taught and the ornament of expression that clothes it, and concedes the palm in eloquence while keeping the substance, leaving his opponents talkativeness without gravity; he pauses to ask whether eloquence is not after all necessary in a teacher, and answers that the apostle was no mere infant in speech. Gill argues that he was not unlearned at all but chose a plainer style accommodated to common people. Ellicott identifies the sneerers not with the Greek party of culture but with the Judaising teachers, and reconstructs their taunt, that a man cutting and stitching all day could hardly be a doctor of the law. Robertson notes that the Greeks used the word of a man who attended to his own affairs and took no part in public life, and Wesley reduces it to speaking in a plain unadorned way.
7:
Ellicott sets out the charge in the form it must have taken. The rival teachers boasted of their disinterestedness, and had detected what they took for an inconsistency: he accepted help from Macedonia while refusing it at Corinth, so that to take money at all was mean and not to take it from them was contemptuous. The apostle does not deny the facts but repeats the irritating word. Clarke calls the whole passage truly ironical and Robertson says it amounts to sarcasm to ask whether he sinned in preaching the gospel free of charge. Calvin observes that a humility deserving of no ordinary commendation was cast up to him as a reproach; Gill lists what the abasement consisted in, the modest bearing, the popular style, and the working at his trade. What their exaltation was they put differently, Wesley making it their becoming children of God and Clarke their receiving the pure doctrines of the gospel and being raised to the highest pitch of light and blessedness.

The verb in the next verse is agreed to be military and its application is not. Barnes gives it as spoiled or plundered and explains that a conqueror gives no equivalent for what he takes, which is the only sense in which the church at Philippi was plundered; Robertson derives it from stripping arms from a slain foe, and Wesley calls it plainly a military term. Ellicott grounds it elsewhere, in wages drawn from one employer while another was served, and notes that the word means rations rather than money, an earlier use of it having perhaps given occasion for the sneer that he can take wages when it suits him. Gill grounds it differently again, in the disparity that those he took from were poor and those he served rich, while insisting there was no injury since the giving was voluntary. Calvin keeps the figure and turns it round: what the churches he had won contributed gratuitously was in a manner due to him by the right of spiritual warfare.

The word for being burdensome is a curiosity and draws three accounts. Barnes reports on Jerome's authority that it is a provincialism of Cilicia, and takes it to mean becoming torpid to another's detriment, so that the apostle did not lead an inactive life at the expense of others. Ellicott traces its history: it is found nowhere else in the New Testament, nor in the Greek Old Testament, nor in any known Greek author but one physician; Jerome's claim is given without proof and must be treated as unproven; and the root is the word for numbness, which gives us narcotic and names a fish of the torpedo kind that benumbs whatever it touches. Robertson counters that its occurrence in that physician suggests a medical term in popular use rather than a local dialect word, and passes on the gloss that the apostle did not benumb the Corinthians by demanding money of them. Calvin notes that the Macedonians did not furnish his living but supplied only what his own labour left wanting; Wesley asks whether the poor have in all ages been more generous than the rich. On the asseveration that follows, Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Calvin all treat it as an oath or all but an oath, Ellicott adding that the verb for stopping means to fence round, so that the boast is said not to have its mouth sealed. Clarke observes that naming the whole province shows he had taken help from no church in it, and Ellicott that the word for region is peculiar to this apostle and is the source of our word climate.
12:
Whether the rival teachers really preached for nothing is the hinge of the twelfth verse, and the voices divide evenly. Calvin says they took no pay at all, making a show of uncommon zeal to allure ignorant people; Ellicott defends the same inference against the objection that there is no evidence for it, answering that where it follows naturally from the language and nothing contradicts it that is evidence enough. Against them Chrysostom is blunt: even that was a falsehood, and they took money but did it secretly. Clarke says it is certain the passage does not mean they took nothing, whatever they pretended, since the apostle is positive to the contrary; Barnes suspects they contrived an ample support under various pretences; Wesley grants they boasted of being burdensome to no man but calls the boast vain in them though not in the apostle.

Chrysostom opens the next verse with a challenge. What sayest thou, he asks, men who preach Christ, who take no money, who bring in no different gospel, and these are called false apostles? Yes, he answers, and for this reason most of all, because they make a pretence of these things in order to deceive; they do work indeed, but pull up what has been planted, and take the mask of truth to enact the drama of error. Calvin puts it in a figure, that it is as if a harlot were to borrow the apparel of a decent matron, and warns that men are not to be received as servants of Christ as soon as any appearance of excellence is discovered. Robertson notes that the verb for the masquerade is played on through three successive verses, men posing as ministers of Christ by putting on the outward habiliments. Ellicott ties the phrase back to the ironical title used earlier.

What the transforming of Satan refers to is disputed. Clarke ties it to Eden, where whatever shape he took his pretensions gave him the appearance of a good angel, and lists three forms in which the tempter comes, the subtle serpent, the roaring lion and the angel of light; Barnes looks to the same scene and to the temptation in the wilderness. Ellicott denies that any single incident is in view, since the tense of the verb makes it a thing continually done, and looks instead to Corinth, conjecturing that the teachers had claimed angelic authority for their gospel, so that a satanic apparition may have been mistaken for an angelic one. Calvin argues from the greater to the less, that if the head of all wicked persons transforms himself his ministers will do no less. Cyril of Jerusalem states it as a general law that vice mimics virtue and the tares strive to be thought wheat, detected by good judges only from the taste, and gives the tempter's motive: not that he may climb back to where he was, for having made his heart hard as an anvil he has a will that cannot repent, but that he may wrap those who live an angelic life in a mist of blindness. On the last verse Ellicott reconstructs what the ministers of righteousness claimed, a righteousness they said the apostle neglected, under the authority of one called the Just; Barnes takes it of the blackest characters putting on the appearance of the greatest sanctity, and Robertson calls it a tragedy to see men in the livery of heaven serve the devil. Gill and Wesley rest, with Calvin, on the end being according to the works.
16:
Ellicott sharpens the word that is repeated here, suggesting that it means rather insane than merely foolish, so that the plea is that they should give him the hearing most men would give even to one they thought out of his mind. Henry grants that boasting of ourselves is usually not only a sign of a proud mind but a mark of folly too, and asks only that due regard be given to what is said. Calvin finds a twofold design, to expose the vanity of men who were such extravagant trumpeters of their own praises, and to expostulate with the Corinthians for shutting him up to a necessity of glorying; had they done their duty, he says, not one word of this would have been said. Robertson observes that the apostle is plainly embarrassed at having to do it, whereas some men can do it with complete composure.

The disclaimer that follows is the difficulty of the passage. Barnes sets out two senses, that he does not speak by inspiration and that he does not speak in imitation of the Lord's example, prefers the second, and reports a third proposal, that the words are not meant seriously but echo the Corinthians' own view. Robertson takes the second and notes that the meekness and gentleness of Christ had been appealed to a chapter earlier; Clarke says the same, that but for the necessity of vindicating his apostleship the glorying would be inconsistent with his profession of humility. Wesley takes the first sense in a qualified form, not by an express command from the Lord though still under the direction of his Spirit. Ellicott meets the question of inspiration directly. He distinguishes this from the earlier passage where a private opinion was set against a rule felt to be divine, since here the line is drawn between human feeling and divine inspiration, and states the dilemma plainly: if what falls on the lower side is inspired, are we not contradicting what is written as inspired, and if it is not, are we not stripping what follows of authority. Calvin puts it more simply, that the disposition had an eye to God though the outward manner might seem unsuitable in a servant of the Lord.

On the irony that follows the voices are unanimous and enjoy it. Barnes passes on the judgment that this is perhaps the most sarcastic sentence the apostle ever penned; Clarke calls it a very fine irony and observes that it would be dishonourable in wise men to fall out with a fool; Wesley calls it a beautiful irony; Robertson passes on the summary that they tolerated tyranny, extortion, craftiness, arrogance, violence and insult. Calvin alone qualifies the address, inferring that the reproof is not aimed at all indiscriminately but at particular persons who had behaved unkindly; and on the list of outrages he sets out three constructions, that they are reproved for enduring nothing, or charged with indolence for submitting to a disgraceful bondage, or that the apostle repeats what had been spitefully said of himself; the second suits his own view, but he yields to the third as commonly received on patristic authority. The third clause divides them. Ellicott holds the supplied words wrong, since they make it a feeble repetition of the one before, and renders it of a man taking them in by guile; Gill, Clarke and Wesley all take it of goods taken away, Clarke of exacted contributions and Wesley of open violence. Barnes draws the general moral, that a false religion always makes slaves and only true Christianity leaves perfect freedom.
21:
Chrysostom pauses to count the disclaimers, listing them one after another from the opening of the chapter, and draws the moral: if after doing everything we ought still to call ourselves unprofitable, what forgiveness can be due to a man who exalts himself when nothing presses him? He adds the image of the Pharisee who suffered shipwreck even in harbour by striking on that rock. Whose reproach is meant in the verse is disputed. Barnes takes it of the apostle's own, the things they counted disgraceful in him, and reports two further proposals, that the disgrace is the Corinthians' or the false teachers'. Ellicott agrees that it is self-disparagement, and hears behind it the taunt at his bodily infirmities, as though it were only weakness that had kept him from the same acts of self-asserting authority. Clarke passes on a paraphrase making it the reproach cast on the Corinthians as profane and uncircumcised. Gill leaves the possibilities open, and Robertson calls the whole intense irony, presented as another man's charge.

The three names that follow were the opponents' boast, and what each claimed is variously given. Clarke makes them language, lineage and covenant standing: those who spoke the sacred tongue and read the Scriptures in it, those descended from Jacob and not from Esau, and those circumcised and in the bond of the covenant, so that he is no proselyte. Ellicott reads them as answers to three separate insinuations: that he was a Hellenist content with the Greek version; that he had no right to the second name at all, being perhaps only the grandson of a proselyte; and that his heathen sympathies were thus accounted for. Henry lists the same privileges more plainly, a family that never intermarried with the Gentiles, descent from Jacob, and the seed of Abraham rather than the proselytes. On the name itself the philologists divide: Gill rejects at length the derivation from Abraham as betraying ignorance of the language, since Abraham himself bears the name; Calvin derives it from Heber on the evidence of Genesis; Barnes from the verb meaning to pass over, applied to Abraham as one come from a foreign land. Calvin adds his contempt for the whole boast, that they had placed the prow and stern of their excellence in a thing so trivial.

At the next title the tone changes. Calvin marks the turn: having scattered their carnal glories like smoke by a breath of wind, and having been content so far to stand level with them, he now separates himself from their society altogether, since to be a minister of Christ is far more honourable than to be first-born among all the posterity of Abraham. Robertson makes the same point from the grammar, that the phrase means not more than I but I more than they. Ellicott and Robertson both note that the word for folly is here sharpened to mean speaking deliriously, and Ellicott takes it again for the very term of insult flung at him. On the imprisonments Robertson reports that an early Roman writer numbered them at seven, that only five are known and only one before this letter, and asks whether there may have been one at Ephesus; Ellicott makes the same count and infers that the historian understates rather than exaggerates these sufferings. Clarke observes that the beatings were at heathen hands, where no rule governed the scourging, and adds the sharpest thrust of the passage, that had he preached circumcision he would have been as free from opposition as they were; Gill notes that he could have denied them the title but conceded it rhetorically, and Wesley that the deaths surrounded him in the most dreadful forms.
24:
Barnes opens the catalogue with remarks that govern the whole of it. The particulars cannot be extracted from the history, which proves that letter and narrative were written independently; and yet no article in the list is contradicted by the history, which has left room enough for all of them. At the stoning he presses further, reporting the judgment that this passage comes nearer to a contradiction without incurring one than any case that writer had met with, since the narrative records one stoning at Lystra and, before it, an assault meant to stone him which was prevented. Ellicott makes the milder form of the same argument, that accuracy where we can check it may fairly be urged as evidence of accuracy where we cannot. Gill corrects the sentimental reading of the thirty-nine: the one stripe was not abated out of tenderness, nor because the offence was thought light, but the utmost rigour of the law was reached as their tradition interpreted it.

The night and day in the deep is the obscurest item. Clarke reports the common supposition of an unrecorded shipwreck in which he saved himself on a plank, and also a theory that the word means a dreadful dungeon in a city of the Propontis, which he thinks unlikely; Ellicott takes the natural sense of one of the shipwrecks just named, and reports the same dungeon theory, comparing the pit into which Jeremiah was let down; Wesley says only that he was probably floating on part of the vessel. Robertson notes that we know nothing of these three wrecks and that the one the history describes came much later.

In the perils Clarke and Ellicott agree that the word rendered waters must be understood of rivers, Ellicott of the swollen torrents that come down in spring from the mountain ranges and Robertson noting that those rivers still rise suddenly in flood. On the robbers Clarke observes that being poor and having nothing to lose he passed unhurt though not without great danger, and Robertson marks the style, the pairs set against each other without preposition or conjunction. Whether the fastings were chosen divides them: Ellicott holds that, set apart from the hunger and thirst just named, they can hardly mean anything but self-chosen abstinence, and Calvin says the same, while Barnes leaves it open as either voluntary or involuntary. Clarke cites a nobleman's reflection on the hardship of all this for a man of liberal education, wandering like a vagabond and almost naked, yet coming into the presence of persons of high life; Wesley makes the same contrast, that he appeared before governors and kings and was not ashamed. Calvin enters a pastoral qualification, that such trials are not indispensably required of all, but that where they appear a greater testimony is afforded, and that a man so distinguished will not on that account despise those less thoroughly tried.

What the things without are is canvassed most fully by Barnes, who reports four proposals and prefers the last, that other things are simply not to be mentioned; Clarke takes it of the outward things just enumerated and Wesley of what he suffered on account of others. On the word that follows all agree it is violent, Barnes giving it as that which rushes upon him and Robertson likening it to the rush of a mob. Ellicott turns it into a picture of the daily routine, the visits of inquirers, the confessions of sin-burdened souls, the craving of perplexed consciences for guidance, the referring of household and church quarrels to his arbitration, and the arrival of messengers from distant churches. Gill and Calvin both set this ordinary burden against the extraordinary ones just listed, and Wesley notes the modesty of saying all the churches rather than the whole church, even those he had never seen.
29:
The pair of questions that follows the care of the churches is read very differently. Ellicott takes both words in their strongest sense: to be made to stumble suggests a grievous sin rather than mere weakness, and the word for burning had been used earlier of the burning of passion, so that he thinks the association clings to it here, and pictures men coming with their tales of shame to a sympathy that entered even there. The others keep it to grief or zeal. Robertson says that when a brother stumbles the apostle is set on fire with grief, and Wesley that he was pained as though he had fire in his bosom; Clarke makes it a zeal to restore the man, and Barnes takes the whole of a deep sympathy with all who need it. Gill spreads the weakness over three kinds, weakness in faith, scrupulousness of conscience, and affliction of body or mind; Calvin observes how many let all offences pass unheeded, which comes of having no concern for the church.

On the resolve to glory in infirmities Clarke attacks a reading he thinks indefensible, that the word means the apostle's indwelling sin, in which he is supposed to have gloried because grace was the more magnified; it would be difficult, he says, to produce one passage in the whole New Testament where the word means sin or moral corruption. Barnes refers it to the sufferings just recounted and to the tenderness of feeling he had admitted, noting that the Stoics counted all sensitiveness to suffering an infirmity. Ellicott sums it up neatly, that he is confident his weak points are stronger than their strong ones; Calvin lists what the world counts contemptible rather than glorious, hunger and imprisonment and stoning and stripes.

Whether the oath that follows looks back or forward divides them. Barnes holds it made in view of the sufferings just recounted, since nothing in the escape at Damascus demanded so solemn an appeal; Clarke and Calvin refer it forward, because the fact was not yet generally known; Gill takes it of both together. Clarke adds that nothing here countenances profane swearing, this appeal being in the same spirit as his most earnest prayer. Ellicott notes that the participle rendered which is is the form used in the Greek Old Testament for the divine name, and conjectures that the attestation was meant to introduce a much fuller narrative than the one that followed.

How Damascus came to be under an Arabian king is answered two ways. Clarke explains it from the war that followed the divorce of that king's daughter by Herod, the emperor's death having saved him from the force sent against him, and conjectures that he then seized a favourable moment; Robertson reports instead the absence of Roman coins there for a stretch of years and the suggestion that a later emperor gave the city to him out of dislike for Herod. Gill supplies a list of the kings who bore the name, and Barnes and Robertson agree that the watch set by the governor and the watch kept by his own countrymen were not rival accounts, the second having procured the first. Why this escape closes the chapter is answered differently again. Ellicott finds an element of the ludicrous in it, something undignified that gave occasion for jests; Robertson calls it a humiliating experience in the city he had entered as a conqueror over the people he now belonged to. Calvin takes it as a first apprenticeship, and answers the objection that flight shows no valiant spirit by observing that the closing of the gates of a royal city showed with what rage his enemies were inflamed. Barnes harmonises the two accounts through an aperture in the wall, and Ellicott and Robertson note that the word used here means a rope-work hamper where the historian uses the general term.
